Pregnancy

Everyday pregnancy precautions: food, medicines and exposures

Updated: October 11, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Pregnancy precautions should help you make informed choices, not make every daily task feel dangerous. Risks depend on the product, activity, amount and your health. Use this guide alongside individual maternity advice; an accidental exposure does not automatically mean harm.

Raw meat, seafood and eggs

Avoid raw or undercooked meat, fish and shellfish; foodborne infections can make you seriously ill and some can harm a pregnancy. Cook to appropriate safe temperatures, keep raw foods separate and wash hands and utensils. A food thermometer is more reliable than meat colour alone.

For eggs, follow the rules where you live. UK guidance permits raw or runny hen eggs from specified safety schemes; otherwise cook eggs thoroughly or use pasteurized egg products in uncooked sauces and desserts. This exception does not apply to every egg or country.

Milk, dairy and soft cheese

Choose pasteurized milk and dairy products. Listeria infection can cause pregnancy loss or severe newborn illness. Not every soft cheese is forbidden: pasteurized cream cheese, mozzarella and similar products are permitted under UK guidance.

Mould-ripened soft and soft blue cheeses may still need cooking until steaming hot even when pasteurized. Hard-cheese exceptions also vary by local advice. Check the actual cheese, label, refrigeration and use-by date rather than relying only on the word “soft” or the country of origin.

Fish: choose species, not a blanket ban

Fish provides useful nutrients, but mercury levels differ by species. FDA/EPA advice supports 2–3 four-ounce servings a week from its “Best Choices” list; local oily-fish and tuna limits may differ. Salmon, sardines and several other options are lower in mercury. This does not guarantee a particular IQ.

Avoid high-mercury choices such as shark, swordfish, marlin, king mackerel and bigeye tuna under FDA advice. King mackerel is different from Atlantic mackerel; flounder and whitefish are not automatically high-mercury species. Check local advisories for caught fish and cook fish safely.

Carrots, vitamin A and organ meats

Carrots contain beta-carotene, which differs from preformed vitamin A such as retinol. Ordinary carrots are not a reason for a pregnancy ban. For carrot juice and other juices, choose pasteurized or otherwise safely treated products; large quantities are not needed for benefit.

Avoid liver and liver products under NHS guidance, and avoid high-retinol supplements or cod-liver oil unless specifically prescribed. Other organ meats are not all nutritionally identical to liver; seek local advice and cook any permitted meat safely. Review supplement ingredients with your clinician.

Sprouts and herbal drinks

Avoid raw sprouts, including home-grown ones: bacteria can be present inside seeds and washing alone may not remove them. Cook sprouts thoroughly. Wash other produce under running water rather than using soap or bleach.

“Natural” does not establish safety. Herbal teas, concentrated extracts and medicinal herbs vary by ingredient and dose, with limited pregnancy evidence. Check each product with a pharmacist or maternity team rather than assuming every tea is safe or every culinary herb causes miscarriage.

Alcohol

There is no known safe amount, type or time for alcohol in pregnancy. Avoid it. Alcohol can affect growth, learning, behaviour, coordination and physical development and cause fetal alcohol spectrum disorders, including fetal alcohol syndrome. Neurological problems can include seizures in some affected children. It also increases risks of loss, stillbirth and preterm birth. Effects vary and are not certain after every exposure.

If you drank before knowing, discuss it without blame and obtain prenatal care. If you may be alcohol-dependent or develop withdrawal when reducing intake, seek medical help promptly for a safe plan rather than abruptly detoxing alone. Severe withdrawal, seizures, confusion or hallucinations need emergency care.

Caffeine

Count caffeine from coffee, tea, cola, energy products, chocolate and medicines or supplements. NHS guidance limits total intake to 200 mg daily; Health Canada uses a 300 mg maximum for pregnancy. These are different national recommendations, not proof that a particular dose has zero risk.

Use local maternity advice and consider the more cautious 200 mg limit when unsure. Serving sizes and brewing methods change the amount substantially, so “two coffees” is not a reliable universal measure. Higher intake has been associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes; one accidental excess does not diagnose harm.

Hair dye

Most research is reassuring about usual hair-dye exposure in pregnancy, which is much lower than doses used in some experiments. Waiting until after 12 weeks is an optional precaution, not evidence that normal first-trimester use necessarily harmed the fetus.

Follow instructions, use gloves, ventilate, perform recommended tests and rinse thoroughly. Do not exceed application time or continue after a reaction. Tell your hairdresser you are pregnant; repeated salon work exposure may need separate occupational advice.

Hot tubs, saunas and overheating

Avoid overheating in hot tubs, saunas, steam rooms or very hot exercise settings. Prolonged high core temperature, especially early in pregnancy, is a concern, while dehydration and fainting can also harm you. Research cannot predict an individual outcome from one exposure.

A comfortably warm bath is different from prolonged overheating. Stay cool, take breaks and drink appropriately in hot weather rather than assuming all outdoor activity or sun exposure is forbidden. Leave the heat if unwell; fever or significant heat illness warrants medical advice.

Paint and renovation

Usual household painting with appropriate precautions is expected to produce low exposure and is unlikely to increase miscarriage or birth-defect risk. Product, duration and ventilation matter; smell alone does not measure dose. Ongoing job exposure differs from a brief household encounter.

Consider having someone else paint. Use suitable products, ventilation and label precautions, and limit time in freshly painted areas. Do not scrape, sand or burn old paint that could contain lead; use qualified removal services. Delaying to another trimester is not a substitute for controlling exposure.

Medicines and supplements

Review prescription medicines, over-the-counter products, vitamins and herbs with a clinician or pharmacist. Some are unsuitable, while others are important treatment. Do not stop a prescribed medicine on your own: untreated illness or sudden withdrawal can harm both you and the pregnancy.

Contact the prescriber promptly when pregnancy is recognized, ideally before conception if possible. Give the exact name, dose and dates of any exposure. A medicine-specific assessment is more useful than a blanket “all medicines are dangerous” rule; complementary products do not replace antenatal care.

Necessary X-rays and dental care

Tell the imaging team and dentist that you are or may be pregnant. Clinically necessary diagnostic X-rays should not be withheld or delayed solely to reach a later trimester. The team chooses the appropriate test and dose, considering the body area, indication and alternatives.

Necessary dental X-rays and treatment can be provided at any stage of pregnancy; delaying an infection or needed treatment can worsen problems. This does not mean every radiation exposure is identical or risk-free. Ask about the specific examination rather than cancelling it yourself.

Sport and lifting

Suitable exercise and adapted strengthening are generally beneficial in an uncomplicated pregnancy. Avoid substantial contact, falls, abdominal blows, scuba diving and overheating. Weight training is not automatically forbidden; previous experience, symptoms and pregnancy complications affect the plan.

Ordinary lifting does not establish a cause of miscarriage. Repeated heavy occupational lifting, awkward loads and prolonged standing may need assessment, help and task changes. There is no single safe weight limit for everyone; obtain specific advice instead of either pushing through pain or stopping all movement.

Pets, litter and soil

You do not generally need to stop caring for all pets. Toxoplasma can be transmitted through contaminated food, soil and cat faeces, and a new infection in pregnancy can affect the fetus, including eye or brain injury or pregnancy loss. A healthy-looking cat does not exclude the risk.

Have someone else change cat litter if possible. Otherwise use disposable gloves, wash hands afterwards and change litter daily. Use gloves for gardening, wash produce, keep cats indoors and do not feed them raw meat. Discuss specific animal or workplace exposures with your clinician or veterinarian.

Smoking, tobacco and secondhand smoke

Avoid smoking and tobacco, including waterpipe smoke, and reduce exposure to other people’s smoke. Smoking is linked to poor fetal growth, preterm birth, placental complications, some birth defects and sudden infant death; secondhand smoke is harmful too.

Vaping is not a harmless pregnancy alternative. Ask for supportive cessation care and advice on appropriate treatments rather than struggling alone. Quitting at any stage can help; needing support is not a reason for shame.

Nonmedical drugs and dependence treatment

Avoid nonmedical drug use and tell your team about substances honestly so they can support you. Risks differ by drug, dose and combinations. Cannabis is not a proven pregnancy remedy, and combining opioids with alcohol or sedatives raises overdose risk.

Do not suddenly stop opioids or prescribed dependence treatment yourself. Methadone or buprenorphine is recommended for many pregnant people with opioid-use disorder, with specialist prenatal care. Treatment medicines are not equivalent to uncontrolled drug use; plans for changes or withdrawal require clinical supervision.

Pesticides and insect repellents

Minimize unnecessary pesticide exposure and, if possible, have someone else mix or apply products. Follow label instructions, protective measures and instructions on leaving and re-entering treated areas. Professional pest treatment does not automatically mean a harmful fetal exposure; assessment depends on the product and dose.

Skin insect repellent is different from spraying a room or crop. CDC considers EPA-registered repellents, including DEET and picaridin, safe in pregnancy when used as directed. Use locally authorized products, clothing and screens; do not apply clothing-treatment permethrin directly to skin.

If exposure or symptoms worry you

Contact your maternity team, pharmacist or a poison-information service for advice about a specific exposure. Keep the product label and note timing and amount. Seek prompt care for fever 38°C or higher, illness after risky food, persistent vomiting or inability to keep fluids down; do not wait for a routine visit.

Get immediate emergency care for breathing difficulty, chest pain, fainting or loss of consciousness, seizures, severe abdominal pain or heavy bleeding. Contact maternity care immediately for leaking fluid or reduced fetal movements. A precaution list cannot diagnose harm, and symptoms take priority over checking an app. Do not drive yourself in an emergency.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Use local pregnancy food advice to check fish species, egg and cheese products, cooking and juice safety. Count caffeine from all drinks, foods, medicines and supplements, and check product labels rather than assuming one rule fits every country.

Ask promptly for individual advice about medicines, imaging or a worrying exposure. Do not stop prescribed treatment yourself or postpone a clinically needed X-ray or dental treatment solely because of pregnancy; tell the team you are pregnant.

Keep product names, ingredient lists, amounts and dates for your maternity team. Ask for support with smoking, alcohol or other substances; dependence needs a supervised plan, not do-it-yourself withdrawal. Seek care for warning signs without waiting for an app record.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help you record foods, medicines, symptoms and questions for your maternity team. It cannot assess a toxic exposure, diagnose fetal harm or replace urgent care; keep product details and seek professional advice when needed.

When to seek help

Get immediate emergency care for breathing difficulty, chest pain, fainting or loss of consciousness, seizures, severe abdominal pain or heavy bleeding. Fever 38°C or higher, illness after a risky food or inability to keep fluids down needs prompt assessment. Contact maternity care immediately for leaking fluid or reduced fetal movements. Do not drive yourself in an emergency.

Evidence notes updated: October 11, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Keep food safety, species-specific fish advice and local egg and cheese rules in mind.
  • Avoid alcohol and tobacco; get supported treatment for dependence rather than detoxing abruptly alone.
  • Review medicines promptly, and do not delay necessary X-rays or dental care solely because of the trimester.
  • Adapt activity and reduce unnecessary exposures; get help promptly for warning symptoms.

Frequently asked questions

Which foods need particular care?

Avoid raw or undercooked meat, fish and shellfish, raw sprouts, unsafe unpasteurized products and high-mercury fish. Egg and cheese exceptions depend on the product and local guidance; suitable cooked foods and many pasteurized dairy products remain options.

Why check herbal teas and remedies?

Safety varies by ingredient, concentration and dose, and evidence may be limited. Ask about the exact product rather than assuming “natural” means safe or that all herbs cause pregnancy loss.

How much caffeine is recommended?

NHS guidance uses no more than 200 mg a day from all sources; Health Canada uses 300 mg. Follow local maternity advice and consider 200 mg when uncertain. Cup size and preparation vary.

Is lifting always forbidden?

No. Appropriate strengthening and ordinary lifting differ from repeated heavy or awkward work. Seek assessment and practical help with demanding loads; there is no universal kilogram limit.

Should necessary X-rays wait until later pregnancy?

No. Tell the team you are pregnant, but do not postpone clinically necessary imaging or dental care solely because of the trimester. The team will assess the specific examination and alternatives.

Are carrots or carrot juice forbidden because of vitamin A?

Carrots contain beta-carotene, not the high-retinol exposure associated with birth-defect risk. Choose pasteurized or safely treated juice; avoid high-retinol supplements and liver according to guidance unless specifically advised otherwise.

Must I stop prescribed medicine or dependence treatment?

Do not stop on your own. Obtain a prompt medicine-specific review. Abrupt opioid withdrawal or unsupported alcohol detoxification can be dangerous; supported clinical treatment is available.

What if I already had an exposure?

An exposure does not automatically establish harm. Note the product, amount and date and obtain specific advice. Fever, significant illness or inability to keep fluids down needs prompt care; breathing difficulty, fainting or loss of consciousness, seizures, severe pain or heavy bleeding needs emergency care. Do not drive yourself in an emergency.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
